concepts.decision: Use when a requirement must survive change, misuse, or component failure.
concepts.definition: Deliberate architecture that reduces exploitable failure paths before deployment.
concepts.failureExample: A feature works in normal testing but has no defined behavior when its authorization service fails.
concepts.label: Secure Design

concepts.decision: Scope each human, service, and admin role to its required action.
concepts.definition: Grant only authority necessary for a defined task and duration.
concepts.failureExample: One deployment account can read every production secret.
concepts.label: Least Privilege

concepts.decision: Choose layers with different failure modes across identity, network, endpoint, and recovery.
concepts.definition: Independent safeguards arranged so one failed control does not expose the asset.
concepts.failureExample: A stolen password reaches sensitive data because no second control checks device or action.
concepts.label: Defense In Depth

concepts.decision: Choose the safe initial state when setup is incomplete or ambiguous.
concepts.definition: Initial configuration that protects the asset without requiring a user to opt in.
concepts.failureExample: A new storage bucket is publicly readable until an owner changes a setting.
concepts.label: Secure Defaults

concepts.decision: Define the safe state for dependency loss, timeout, or malformed input.
concepts.definition: Behavior that denies or limits unsafe action when a security decision cannot be made.
concepts.failureExample: An authorization timeout causes a gateway to allow the request.
concepts.label: Fail Securely

concepts.decision: Separate request, approval, implementation, and review where fraud or error matters.
concepts.definition: Division of conflicting authority so one role cannot complete a sensitive action alone.
concepts.failureExample: The same administrator requests, deploys, and approves a payment-rule change.
concepts.label: Separation Of Duties

concepts.decision: Re-evaluate access at a meaningful request or session boundary.
concepts.definition: Access approach that evaluates identity, device, context, and request instead of trusting network location.
concepts.failureExample: An internal subnet lets a compromised workstation call an admin API.
concepts.label: Zero Trust

concepts.decision: Ask what personal data is needed for the stated purpose and lifecycle.
concepts.definition: Design practice that makes purpose, minimization, and accountability part of the system.
concepts.failureExample: A feature collects precise location forever for a one-time delivery estimate.
concepts.label: Privacy By Design

concepts.decision: Map every layer and control to an accountable operator and verifier.
concepts.definition: Explicit allocation of security operation and assurance duties among parties.
concepts.failureExample: A customer assumes a provider configured tenant sharing and alerting.
concepts.label: Shared Responsibility

concepts.decision: Use before design commitment and when a material boundary or dependency changes.
concepts.definition: Structured examination of assets, actors, data flows, trust boundaries, abuse cases, and assumptions.
concepts.failureExample: An API accepts a partner callback without modeling replay or forged requests.
concepts.label: Threat Modeling

concepts.decision: Prefer the smallest architecture that meets the stated requirement; justify each added dependency, interface, and privilege.
concepts.definition: Reduce unnecessary components, privileges, states, and interactions so the design can be understood, tested, and operated.
concepts.failureExample: A convenience integration creates unreviewed state transitions and a hidden administrative bypass.
concepts.label: Keep It Simple And Small

concepts.decision: Use when identity-aware access, traffic steering, and policy enforcement at distributed edges fit the data flow and service boundary.
concepts.definition: An architecture delivering integrated network and security access controls at distributed user, branch, and application edges.
concepts.failureExample: A team assumes SASE replaces application authorization and leaves a broad API role unchanged.
concepts.label: Secure Access Service Edge

misconceptions.claim: Defense in depth means adding many overlapping products.
misconceptions.correction: Layers should address different failure paths and have understandable ownership and evidence.

misconceptions.claim: Buying SASE makes every application zero trust.
misconceptions.correction: A service label does not establish resource-level authorization, correct policy, endpoint posture, or operational evidence. Validate each relevant boundary and action.

outcome: Recommend secure design principles for a stated architecture tradeoff and explain the failure they reduce.

sections.body: Least privilege narrows what a subject or service can do. Defense in depth avoids reliance on one control. Secure defaults make the safer state the initial state. Fail-secure behavior denies or limits action when a required security decision cannot be made. Separation of duties reduces conflicting power, while simplicity reduces hidden assumptions and review burden.
keyPoints: Use several principles together against a specific failure path.
Availability requirements may need carefully designed fail-safe behavior; state the tradeoff.
sections.title: Principles constrain failure paths

sections.body: Zero trust treats access as a continually evaluated decision rather than a location-based entitlement. Privacy by design brings collection, purpose, minimization, and accountability into design. Shared responsibility assigns which party secures each layer in a service model. Threat modeling tests whether these assumptions hold across data flows, trust boundaries, operations, and change.
keyPoints: A cloud provider’s responsibility does not remove the customer’s responsibility for configuration and data use.
Trust boundaries and ownership must be explicit.
sections.title: Architecture includes ownership and trust

sections.body: Threat modeling exposes assets, actors, data flows, trust boundaries, abuse cases, and assumptions before implementation. Least privilege limits each subject or service to necessary actions; defense in depth covers independent failure paths; secure defaults make protection the initial state; and fail-secure behavior limits unsafe action when a security dependency fails. Segregation of duties separates conflicting authority, while keeping designs simple and small reduces hidden interactions. Traditional trust-but-verify can retain broad trust after initial authentication. Zero trust grants no implicit trust solely from network location or ownership; authentication and authorization precede resource access and decisions use relevant evidence. privacy by design constrains collection and use early; shared responsibility assigns each service-layer control; and secure access service edge (SASE) delivers integrated network and security access controls at distributed user, branch, and application edges. Select SASE where its identity-aware access, traffic steering, and policy enforcement boundaries meet the use case; it does not replace application authorization, endpoint security, or responsibility for policy configuration. Each principle needs an owner, test, and stated availability or usability tradeoff; slogans without those details create untested trust.
keyPoints: State the protected property, boundary, decision owner, operating evidence, and residual failure mode.
Treat architecture controls as lifecycle commitments: configuration, monitoring, response, maintenance, and recovery determine whether the claim holds.
sections.title: Apply every secure-design principle to a decision and failure path

sections.body: SASE combines WAN connectivity and cloud-delivered security services for distributed access. Typical capabilities include SD-WAN, secure web gateways, CASB, firewall services, and identity-aware application access. Compare traffic paths, enforcement locations, identity/device signals, resilience, logging, provider responsibilities, and application needs before adoption. Edge access approval does not authorize every application action. Keeping a design simple and small means eliminating unnecessary interfaces and states so people can reason about, test, and operate it; it does not mean removing required protection. A SASE rollout with many overlapping exceptions can remain complex and overprivileged.
keyPoints: Zero trust is a set of trust and access principles; SASE is a network/security delivery architecture that can support them.
Justify each interface and exception against the requirement, failure behavior, and evidence needed to operate it.
sections.title: Separate access architecture, trust assumptions, and design complexity
